title: When Modelling, Do an Example in Real-Time
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton reflects on a gap in his own well-known Silent Teacher modelling routine: students never actually see him perform a procedure at normal speed, start to finish. Because Silent Teacher deliberately slows down at each step to give students time to think, and the We Do phase slows things down further by working line by line on mini-whiteboards, a 20-second procedure ends up looking like a 2-minute one. He identifies two risks of this: students may believe the procedure is harder than it is, and they may never build the fluency and automaticity needed to free up attention for more complex problems. His fix is not to abandon slow, deliberate modelling, but to add a final real-time run-through after the thinking and reflection have happened, so students can see what fluent expert performance actually looks like and have something concrete to aspire to.
points: Barton identifies a blind spot in deliberately slow modelling routines like Silent Teacher: students never see a procedure performed at its true, real-world speed.

He names two concrete risks of always-slow modelling: it can make a procedure look harder than it is, and it can stop students from developing the fluency and automaticity needed for more complex problems.
His fix isn't to cut the slow, step-by-step modelling — it's to add a real-time run-through afterward, once students have already thought hard about each step.
The real-time demonstration is framed as showing students 'what they can aspire towards,' turning fluency itself into a visible teaching goal.
quotes: Here I want to reflect on a mistake I have still been making after all these years: students never get to see me perform a procedure in real-time.
During Silent Teacher I deliberately go slowly, pausing at critical points to give my students an opportunity to consider what I have just done, and what I might do next.
Because students never get to see me perform a procedure in real-time, a 20-second procedure actually comes across as a 2-minute procedure.
Performing a procedure slowly and methodically may give the impression that it is harder than it actually is, which may put off some students.
By performing a procedure slowly and methodically, students may never develop the fluency and automaticity necessary to free up attention to use that skill to solve more complex problems
Now, none of this is to say we should rush through the modelling phase. Of course, it is crucial we slow down and draw students’ attention to critical parts of the process.

For me, this comes after Silent Teacher and the subsequent reflection, but before the We Do: “Now we have thought hard about this, let’s watch it play out in real time”. This shows our students what they can aspire towards.
